title: Guide, Not Bind: Why Defeasible Priors Fail in Augmented Lagrangian Causal Discovery
abstract: Differentiable causal discovery methods increasingly encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints enforced by an Augmented Lagrangian (ALM) penalty, on the assumption that a data-adaptive relaxation mechanism will discount and eventually override a rule the data consistently contradicts. We show this design, which we call \emph{guide, not bind}, fails for two independent, precisely characterized reasons, and that directly repairing both restores it only partially. First, sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses a wrongly-forbidden true edge before any counterfactual check can detect it: we give three necessary conditions any adaptive relaxation must satisfy to avoid this (Proposition~\ref{prop:conditions}), prove that DADU---the natural relaxation rule this paper introduces as the object of study---violates all three (Corollary~\ref{cor:dadu_failure}), and confirm the failure across 3{,}072 training runs spanning graphs from 4 to 32 nodes, where a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge in 87--97\% of trials under DADU. Second, and independent of any fix to the mechanism, we prove in closed form that the standard correlation-matching objective ties a true edge and its reverse to an identical cost of exactly $2r^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tie}), not because the underlying equal-variance model is unidentifiable, but because normalizing to correlation discards exactly the variance information that would make it identifiable; covariance matching instead separates the two directions by a provable margin of at least $w_0^4$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:separation}).

title: Topology-Aware Encrypted Collective Communication for Multi-Node Confidential Hpc Clusters
abstract: Configuring secure communication between collectives is critical for clusters configuration that are used for sensitive scientific, medical, financial and defence workloads to communicate privately. But the traditional MPI-based inter-node communication can still suffer from eavesdropping, alteration of messages, replaying and violation of the communication. Uniform encryption ensures encryption of transmitted data, yet has an included substantial level of delay, calculation burden and scalability constraints. This work presents an encrypted framework for the collective communication that takes into account topology and provides mutual optimization with respect to communication security and performance. This framework combines topology discovery, key authentication, secure management of group keys, adaptation of collective algorithms, and collective message processing to be pipelined. It determines appropriate tree, ring, recursive-doubling or hierarchical communication strategies based on the message size, network topology, congestion, and cost of encryption. Experimental evaluation for multiple nodes Broadcast, Reduce, AllReduce, AllGather, and AlltoAll operations. Findings show improved performance in terms of reduced latency, encryption overhead, throughput and scaling, as well as tamper detection, replay detection and unauthorised nodes detection, which all contribute to secure and performance efficient confidential HPC deployments under a realistic workload environment.

title: Adaptive Geometry Transformation via Genetic Algorithm Simulation
abstract: This paper explores the application of a genetic algorithm to optimize geometric transformations, offering a novel approach to simulating complex physical phenomena such as molecular motion and fluid flow. Traditional geometric transformation methods rely on predefined rules, while this study leverages the algorithm's inherent randomness to discover more effective transformations. The core mechanism involves genetic operators such as crossover and mutation to refine the transformation process, ultimately leading to improved simulation accuracy and the ability to model intricate physical systems. This work presents a framework for automating the optimization of geometric parameters, enhancing the fidelity of numerical simulations.

title: Quantum Geometry: Dynamic Topology Analysis for Quantum Information Processing
abstract: Quantum geometry, a burgeoning field combining quantum mechanics and topology, offers a novel approach to understanding and manipulating quantum information. This paper explores the development of a dynamic topology analysis method, leveraging the principles of quantum geometry, to investigate the behavior of quantum information processing systems. We propose a framework predicated on the inherent stability and adaptability of quantum systems, aiming to predict the robustness of quantum algorithms through the analysis of topology. This research will address key challenges in characterizing and optimizing the performance of quantum systems, ultimately contributing to the advancement of quantum information technologies. The core mechanism centers on applying a dynamic topology approach to uncover subtle correlations and vulnerabilities within quantum states, potentially leading to significant improvements in computational accuracy and efficiency. This work represents a significant step towards a more comprehensive understanding of quantum information processing.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks through Adaptive Symmetry Constraints
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to enhancing the robustness of neural networks against noise and adversarial attacks through the incorporation of adaptive symmetry constraints. The core idea is to dynamically adjust symmetry penalties based on the network's learning progress and the perceived level of internal noise. Unlike traditional adversarial training methods which are often reactive, our approach proactively encourages symmetry within the network's activations and gradients. We introduce a mathematical framework that formalizes this concept, detailing the constraints, the adaptive penalty modulation mechanism, and the theoretical underpinnings of the approach. The proposed method demonstrates the potential to improve network stability and resilience without requiring extensive labeled adversarial data. The key contributions of this work are the adaptive symmetry constraint mechanism and the theoretical justification for its effectiveness.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Tensor Field Theory for Gravitational Waves
abstract: Quantum-enhanced Tensor Field Theory (QETF) offers a novel framework for predicting gravitational wave patterns, potentially significantly improving the accuracy of gravitational wave detection. This paper details the design and implementation of a quantum algorithm to simulate the evolution of the gravitational field, specifically targeting subtle correlations that classical methods often overlook. We explore the advantages of quantum computation in capturing these correlations, aiming to overcome limitations imposed by classical computational resources and provide a fundamentally new approach to gravitational wave analysis. The paper outlines the algorithm's core mechanism, including the use of a parameterized quantum state space and a carefully constructed quantum circuit to represent the gravitational field dynamics. We present preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's potential to enhance detection capabilities and offer a promising path towards more precise gravitational wave observations.

title: Quantum Entanglement States: A Novel Geometric Transformation
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a fascinating phenomenon where two or more particles become linked in such a way that they share the same fate, no matter how far apart they are. This seemingly paradoxical connection has profound implications for quantum computing and quantum information processing. This paper explores the potential of manipulating quantum entanglement through novel geometric transformations, specifically investigating how these transformations can be used to model and control quantum systems. We propose a '纠缠几何' transformation, which leverages the inherent properties of entangled states to create new geometric structures with potentially transformative effects on quantum computation. The core mechanism centers around the mathematical formulation of this transformation, aiming to reveal a fundamentally new approach to simulating and manipulating quantum systems. This research aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between quantum mechanics and geometry, opening avenues for developing more robust and efficient quantum algorithms.

title: Relational Reinforcement Learning with Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but it often struggles when faced with environments that demand intricate reasoning about relationships between elements. This research proposes a novel approach – Relational Reinforcement Learning with Knowledge Graphs (RRLKG) – to address this limitation. The core idea is to augment the RL agent with a knowledge graph, providing it with a structured representation of the environment and enabling it to learn and reason about relationships between objects, actions, and states. We hypothesize that by incorporating this relational reasoning capability, the RL agent's ability to generalize to new environments will be significantly improved. This paper outlines the RRLKG framework, detailing the integration process, the knowledge graph representation, and the resulting RL algorithm. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline future research directions.

title: Predictive Coding with Hierarchical Temporal Memory and Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel predictive coding architecture that leverages the strengths of Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to address the limitations of traditional predictive coding models in capturing long-range temporal dependencies. The core idea is to utilize HTM's internal models to provide a foundational representation for RNNs, allowing the system to learn and predict temporal patterns over extended time horizons. The architecture is designed to overcome the challenges faced by standard predictive coding, which often struggle with the complexities of dynamic environments and the need to integrate past information effectively. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance in predicting and understanding sequences, showcasing the potential of this combined approach for applications in areas such as robotics, time series analysis, and anomaly detection. This work presents a theoretical framework and outlines the key components of the proposed system, setting the stage for future research and development.

title: Quantum Error Correction Protocols: A Probabilistic Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Quantum error correction is a critical requirement for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation. Traditional approaches often rely on precise quantum state manipulation, which is inherently challenging. This paper proposes a novel quantum error correction protocol based on probabilistic optimization, leveraging the inherent distribution of quantum states to dynamically adjust the computation's outcome. We aim to design a self-adaptive optimization strategy that enhances quantum algorithm accuracy and efficiency. This approach moves away from the limitations of deterministic algorithms and embraces the inherent randomness of quantum mechanics. The core mechanism involves introducing noise into the quantum state, guiding the algorithm's evolution to minimize error. This novel design offers a fundamentally different perspective on error correction, potentially achieving significantly improved accuracy and computational speed. The paper details the proposed protocol, presents preliminary results, and discusses future research directions.

title: Algorithmic Proof of Concept for Stable Vector Spaces
abstract: The problem of proving the existence of stable vector spaces within complex functional spaces is a significant challenge in the field of functional analysis. Traditional approaches often involve extensive mathematical derivations and proofs, which can be computationally demanding and time-consuming. This paper proposes an algorithmic proof of concept for a novel method leveraging probabilistic verification based on quantum-enhanced measurements to demonstrate stability without relying on exhaustive mathematical proofs. The core mechanism involves constructing a probabilistic verification scheme that leverages the inherent properties of quantum measurements to effectively assess the stability of vector spaces. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, aiming for a more efficient and direct verification process.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed reasoning engine leveraging quantum entanglement for enhanced computational capabilities and reduced latency. The core claim centers around utilizing entanglement-mediated information transfer between distributed nodes to achieve superluminal communication and facilitate collaborative reasoning. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a network of quantum processors interconnected via entangled qubits, enabling parallel computation and distributed inference. This approach fundamentally departs from classical information transfer limitations, offering a pathway to genuine distributed parallel computation. We outline the theoretical framework, detailing the key mathematical formulations underpinning the system's operation, including entanglement generation, state transfer, and logical operations. The potential impact of this technology on complex problem-solving and distributed systems is significant, though practical realization remains a considerable challenge. We present a foundational model, focusing on the theoretical underpinnings and omitting experimental validation.

title: 基于量子态的自适应神经网络
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture, termed "Quantum-Aware Adaptive Neural Network" (QANN), which leverages quantum computing principles to dynamically adjust network parameters during training. Traditional neural networks often struggle with optimal parameter settings, leading to suboptimal performance. QANN utilizes quantum circuits to represent and manipulate the input data, enabling a more adaptive and efficient training process. The core mechanism centers around quantum state manipulation to achieve enhanced generalization and predictive accuracy. We explore the potential of QANN to overcome these limitations and provide a promising approach to improve deep learning models. The paper details the design of the QANN architecture, the quantum algorithm employed, and the results obtained through simulations and preliminary experiments. Finally, we discuss the implications of this approach and future research directions.

title: Based on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes Distributed Database Design
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to designing secure distributed databases by leveraging quantum error-correcting codes. Traditional distributed databases face vulnerabilities to data corruption and unauthorized access. This research proposes encoding database data into quantum error-correcting codes, utilizing distributed storage and the inherent correction capabilities of these codes to achieve fault-tolerant data storage and retrieval. The core mechanism involves mapping database records to quantum states within a chosen error-correcting code, enabling detection and correction of errors introduced during storage or transmission. We explore the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach, emphasizing enhanced data security and resilience against various attack vectors. evidence.title: Based on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes Distributed Database Design
evidence.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to designing secure distributed databases by leveraging quantum error-correcting codes. Traditional distributed databases face vulnerabilities to data corruption and unauthorized access. This research proposes encoding database data into quantum error-correcting codes, utilizing distributed storage and the inherent correction capabilities of these codes to achieve fault-tolerant data storage and retrieval. The core mechanism involves mapping database records to quantum states within a chosen error-correcting code, enabling detection and correction of errors introduced during storage or transmission. We explore the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach, emphasizing enhanced data security and resilience against various attack vectors. The design considers the challenges associated with implementing quantum error correction in a distributed environment and proposes strategies for optimizing performance and scalability. This work contributes to the emerging field of quantum-secured data management and lays the groundwork for future research in this area.

title: Domain-Coref: A Chinese Benchmark for Extended Anaphoric Phenomena
abstract: Domain-Coref is a document-level Chinese identity-coreference benchmark spanning five discourse domains and five anaphoric phenomena: personal pronouns, demonstratives, definite noun phrases, zero pronouns, and event mentions. It integrates conventional entity reference, zero anaphora, and event reference within a unified identity-coreference framework. The release contains 2,241 documents, 15,959 sentences, 22,510 mentions, and 9,659 identity-coreference chains. It includes the frozen corpus, fixed train/dev/test splits, retained-zero and surface-only CoNLL representations, document-, chain-, mention-, and token-level mappings, and validation metadata for reproducible evaluation.

title: Quantum State Self-Associating Degree Control
abstract: Quantum state self-associating degree control is a novel approach to controlling quantum states, aiming to enhance computational efficiency through dynamic adjustment of the state's self-associating properties. This paper introduces a new algorithm that leverages the unique characteristics of quantum states to automatically optimize self-associating degrees, offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum system control compared to existing static methods. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of this technique in controlling specific quantum states. The core mechanism centers around a sophisticated analysis of quantum state self-associating patterns, enabling the algorithm to dynamically adjust the state's self-associating degree to achieve desired computational outcomes. The algorithm's potential impact extends to a wide range of quantum computing applications, including quantum algorithm optimization and the development of more robust quantum systems.

title: Quantum Reconstruction Algorithm
abstract: Quantum reconstruction algorithms represent a significant advancement in the field of quantum information processing, offering the potential to reconstruct complex quantum states from a single measurement. This paper explores the development of a novel quantum reconstruction algorithm, designed to efficiently restore quantum systems and predict quantum parameter values. We present a robust and scalable approach leveraging quantum state analysis and rapid reconstruction capabilities, addressing the limitations of existing methods. The core mechanism centers around a quantum state reconstruction process that minimizes computational overhead while maximizing accuracy.

title: Geometry-Based Neural Networks for Adaptive Feature Selection
abstract: The efficacy of machine learning models is profoundly influenced by the quality of input data. Feature selection, a crucial preprocessing step, plays a vital role in enhancing model performance and reducing computational complexity. This paper introduces a novel geometric probability neural network designed to automatically select the most relevant features, thereby optimizing model performance and efficiency. The core mechanism of this network leverages the inherent properties of geometric probability to guide the feature selection process, offering a significant advancement over conventional methods. We present a comprehensive analysis demonstrating the superior performance of the proposed architecture across a range of datasets.

title: Dimension Quantum Error Correction Protocol
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a critical component of quantum computing, enabling the reliable transmission of quantum information. Current QEC protocols often rely on computationally intensive calibration and correction steps, limiting the scalability and robustness of quantum devices. This paper proposes a novel dimension quantum error correction protocol based on dynamic dimension mapping, offering a significant advancement over existing approaches. This protocol leverages the inherent properties of quantum systems to dynamically adjust the quantum state's dimensionality, providing enhanced control and measurement fidelity. The core mechanism involves implementing a 'dynamic dimension mapping' technique that establishes a strong correlation between the quantum state's dimension and its measurement outcome. This allows for a more precise control of the quantum state and enables more detailed and accurate quantum measurements. This approach has the potential to address limitations of current QEC protocols, unlocking new possibilities in quantum computing and quantum information security.

title: Title: Quantum Geometry as a Fundamental Algorithm for Computational Complexity
abstract: Quantum Geometry represents a paradigm shift in computational complexity theory, proposing that the inherent geometry of computational spaces can be exploited to efficiently perform computations. This paper explores the potential of quantum geometry as a fundamental algorithm for designing and analyzing complex computational landscapes, offering a fundamentally new approach to algorithm design. We will delve into the core mechanism of constructing quantum circuits that explicitly model geometric properties, demonstrating its capacity to efficiently compute and analyze computational complexity. The paper will outline the conceptual framework, proposed circuit design, and preliminary results suggesting significant advancements over existing computational methods. We conclude with a discussion of future research directions and the potential impact of this novel approach on the field of algorithm design.

title: 基于混沌的自适应几何优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to geometric optimization, leveraging the principles of chaos theory to dynamically adjust the geometry of an object. The algorithm, termed "Adaptive Chaos Optimization" (ACO), utilizes a dynamical system simulation to iteratively refine a geometric shape based on input data. The core mechanism centers around the creation and manipulation of a chaotic system that continuously optimizes a performance metric, offering a significant departure from traditional static optimization techniques. This paper explores the potential of ACO to optimize geometric shapes for specific applications, particularly those requiring dynamic adaptation to changing environmental conditions. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of simulations focusing on optimizing the structural integrity of a cylindrical shape subjected to varying stress levels. The results reveal a notable improvement in the optimized shape's resistance to deformation, demonstrating the potential of ACO for complex geometric optimization.

title: Explainable and Interpretable Vision Models for Trust and Accountability in Real-World Image Processing Systems
abstract: As computer vision systems are increasingly used in safety-critical and real-world settings, explainability is essential for trust, accountability, and responsible deployment. This chapter explores explainable and interpretable AI techniques for image processing, including gradient-based methods like saliency maps and Grad-CAM, as well as concept-based explanations, counterfactual reasoning, and model-agnostic approaches such as LIME and SHAP. It highlights how interpretability supports debugging, bias detection, regulatory compliance, uncertainty estimation, and human-in-the-loop decision-making. The chapter also examines integrating explainability into deployment pipelines, MLOps workflows, and monitoring systems. Key challenges discussed include robustness, computational efficiency, and trade-offs between interpretability and model performance. Through real-world applications, it demonstrates how explainability enhances transparency and reliability, ultimately providing a roadmap for building trustworthy and deployable computer vision systems.

title: Attention-Enhanced Autoencoder with Marginal-Variance-Regularized Feature Reconstruction for Imbalanced Insurance Policy-Ownership Classification
abstract: Identifying the small group of customers who hold a given policy in severely imbalanced tabular data is a recurring screening problem in insurance analytics. This study considers binary caravan-insurance policy-ownership classification on the COIL 2000 benchmark, where the positive-class prevalence is below 6%. The benchmark is a single cross-section, so the label describes current ownership rather than a future purchase event. We propose an Attention-based Symmetric AutoEncoder (ASAE) that combines an auxiliary symmetric reconstruction branch, a channel attention gate, and a marginal log-variance regularizer on a 32-dimensional latent representation. The regularizer operates on individual latent variances and is treated as a heuristic rather than as an estimator of joint differential entropy. Under a common tuning and evaluation protocol on a stratified partition, the ASAE is compared with five conventional machine learning methods and seven neural models. Across five paired runs, it achieves an F1-score of 0.6008 ± 0.0115 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.8584 ± 0.0034. Relative to TabNet, the strongest baseline considered, the mean differences are 0.064 in F1-score (95% confidence interval 0.043-0.085) and 0.032 in AUC (95% confidence interval 0.017-0.048). The ordering is preserved across five stratified re-splits, four imbalance-handling configurations, and a complete type-consistent preprocessing rerun in which nominal attributes are one-hot encoded, oversampled with SMOTENC, and reconstructed with categorical cross-entropy losses (F1-score 0.6241 ± 0.0074, AUC 0.8702 ± 0.0050). All reported results use stratified random partitions of COIL 2000. Because 27% of the records share an identical predictor vector with another record, the official challenge separation and two grouped partitions are also defined, so that exact-duplicate and sociodemographic overlap can be isolated from the primary split. The training code, split indices, and per-run predictions used for the reported tables are publicly available.

title: BizSage: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Framework for Business Research with Efficient Knowledge Retrieval
abstract: While multi-agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating the progressive workflow of academic research, extending them to economics and business research, where specialized domain knowledge spans neighboring disciplines yet remains difficult to access in a structured way, presents two challenges. First, existing methods mostly retrieve at the paper level, yet the evidence needed for research tasks is often distributed across different sections, creating a granularity mismatch that hinders retrieval coverage and precision. Second, these fields demand strict empirical rigor, yet current systems provide limited mechanisms for learning from evaluation feedback. We present \textbf{BizSage}, a multi-agent framework combining corpus-level fine-grained retrieval with quality-driven self-evolution. We build a Lateral Knowledge Graph (LKG) by merging section-level knowledge graphs and apply Personalized PageRank (PPR) to surface semantically relevant and structurally important sections. Seven specialized agents collaborate under a Meta-Review self-evolution mechanism that distills failure modes from evaluation traces into reusable strategies. On a benchmark spanning four domains and three tasks, BizSage ranks first on the majority of metrics, achieves pairwise win-rates above 60\% against six baselines, and produces zero hallucinated citations. We hope BizSage paves the way for reliable research assistance in economics, business, and the broader social sciences.

title: The microscope is the mask: privileged views and labels from a cryo-ET forward model
abstract: We explore the use of simulated data for training a model for protein annotation in crowded cryo-electron tomography volumes reconstructed from images collected at limited tilt angles and severely corrupted by the measurement operator. Firstly, we leverage the corruptions imposed by the forward model to generate domain-specific augmented paired views of the exact same scene for an invariance objective integrated into the LeJEPA self-supervised training framework. Secondly, we use additional information from the simulation pipeline such as the positions and identity of proteins in the simulated volumes to inform the architecture of the model and the loss function, so that semantic information is localised at protein positions in the resulting dense feature volume. The resulting model, CARNIVAL, is evaluated without finetuning on classification and detection tasks in real tomograms, using a benchmark dataset containing multiple protein types and two tomogram processing types. We show that CARNIVAL outperforms a state-of-the-art model trained using a contrastive objective on simulated data but without forward model-based paired views or privileged information.

title: Relative Prime Factorization and Finite-State Presentations under Fixed Finite-Monoid Observation
abstract: Let $L\subseteqΣ^*$ and fix a morphism $h:Σ^*\to M$ into a finite monoid. We study exact factorization and canonical presentation in the relative syntactic congruence $θ_{L,h}:=\equiv_L\cap\ker h$. We separate unique factorization from finite direct presentation. An exhaustively computer-checked $36$-element quotient has a unique exact prime factorization for every live non-unit class, yet its valid prime-return rules contain an infinite family, so unique factorization does not imply the finite relative presentation property (FRP), even for a finite quotient. We lift the same defect to a nonregular context-free language with an infinite relative quotient and finite prime spectrum. To isolate the obstruction, we introduce the finite-state relative presentation property (FSRP), in which canonical valid right-hand-side languages are represented by finite residual controllers, and prove $\mathrm{FRP}\subsetneq\mathrm{FSRP}$. We then introduce prime-target left-division determinism (PTLD), which implies unique exact factorization, tail exactness, tail determinism, and a quadratic bound on valid rules. A nonregular deterministic context-free example with a finite group observer satisfies PTLD while lying outside every fixed $(k,\ell)$-substitutable class. Finally, for fixed $h$ we give a strong positive-data learner for the canonical PTLD presentation with polynomial-time hypothesis updates and a finite characteristic sample, together with a limit reconstruction of the canonical FSRP controller from weakly behaviorally correct CFG-valued learners.

title: Deep learning-based robust autonomous navigation of aerial robots in dense forests
abstract: Autonomous aerial navigation in dense natural environments remains challenging due to limited visibility, thin and irregular obstacles, GNSS-denied operation, and frequent perceptual degradation. This work presents an improved deep learning–based navigation framework that integrates semantically enhanced depth encoding with neural motion-primitive evaluation for robust flight in cluttered forests. Several modules were incorporated on top of the original sevae-ORACLE algorithm, to address limitations observed during real-world deployment, including lateral control for sharper maneuvering, a temporal-consistency mechanism to suppress oscillatory planning decisions, a stereo-based VIO solution for drift-resilient state estimation, and a supervisory safety layer that filters unsafe actions in real time. A depth-refinement stage was additionally included to improve the representation of thin branches and reduce stereo noise, while GPU optimization increased onboard inference throughput from 4 Hz to 10 Hz. To contextualize system performance, a comparative evaluation was conducted against several existing learning-based navigation methods tested under identical environmental conditions and hardware constraints. The proposed approach demonstrated consistently higher success rates, more stable trajectories, and improved collision avoidance, particularly in highly cluttered forest settings. The system was deployed on a custom quadrotor in three boreal forest environments. In moderate-clutter and dense environments, it achieved fully autonomous completion in all 15/15 flights, while in a highly dense underbrush setting it succeeded in 12/15 trials, representing a substantial improvement over the previous baseline, which completed only 5/15 comparable missions. These findings demonstrate that the proposed system provides a measurable improvement in reliability and safety over existing navigation methods in complex natural environments.

title: Minimization of Memory Usage in Multicore System Using Ant Colony Optimization (ACO)
abstract: The accelerated advancement of multicore processor architectures has significantly improved computational performance through parallel task execution. However, increased core integration has amplified challenges related to memory usage and cache contention limitations. Inefficient task-to-core mapping often results in excessive memory consumption, imbalance across cores, and degraded system performance. This paper addresses the problem of memory usage minimization in multicore systems by proposing a memory-aware task scheduling model based on Ant Colony Optimization (ACO). The study formulates the memory minimization problem as a combinatorial optimization model with the objective of reducing total memory usage while maintaining balanced memory distribution across processor cores and satisfying memory capacity constraints. A mathematical framework was developed incorporating decision variables, objective functions, and constraints that capture memory allocation behavior in multicore environments. Within the ACO framework, artificial ants iteratively construct feasible task–core assignments guided by pheromone trails and heuristic information. A memory-aware fitness function integrating total memory usage and memory imbalance is designed to evaluate solution quality. The proposed model was implemented in Python and evaluated using a worked numerical example and simulation experiments. Simulation result shows that fitness improve from 0.001370 to 0.00139 by iteration 3 and stabilizes thereafter indication convergence. The findings confirm that the ACO-based approach effectively minimizes memory usage, reduces imbalance, and satisfies architectural constraints in multicore systems. The study contributes a structured and computationally efficient framework for memory-aware scheduling and provides a foundation for further research in resource optimization for modern multicore architectures.

title: Adaptive Neural Network Based Dynamic Topological Structure
abstract: This paper explores the application of a novel adaptive neural network architecture leveraging dynamic topology to enhance network performance and stability. Traditional neural networks often require manual design, limiting their adaptability and potential for optimization. We introduce a dynamic topology structure that allows the network to automatically adjust its connections based on data distribution, leading to improved expressiveness and robustness. The core mechanism centers around the continuous evolution of the network topology, achieved through a carefully designed dynamic adjustment process. title: A Differential Privacy Framework for Federated Learning
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training machine learning models on decentralized data, addressing privacy concerns by keeping data localized. However, traditional FL approaches often lack robust privacy protection, exposing sensitive user information during model aggregation. This paper proposes a novel framework integrating Differential Privacy (DP) into the FL process. Our framework introduces a DP mechanism within the model aggregation step, guaranteeing that the aggregated model does not reveal information about any individual user's data. We formally define the framework and analyze its privacy-utility trade-off, demonstrating improved privacy guarantees compared to standard FL. This work provides a significant step towards realizing truly private and secure FL systems.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Quantum State Simulation
abstract: Quantum state simulation is a cornerstone of quantum computing, aiming to accurately represent and manipulate the behavior of quantum systems. However, traditional methods of quantum state simulation, such as the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) method and the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), often suffer from significant computational challenges, particularly as the size of the quantum system increases. This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum state simulation leveraging the power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We represent a quantum state as a graph, where nodes correspond to individual quantum states and edges represent the correlations between them. A GNN is then trained to learn the complex relationships within the quantum state, enabling efficient and scalable simulation. Our method significantly reduces the computational burden associated with traditional techniques, offering a promising path towards practical quantum state simulation. The core claim is the utilization of graph neural networks' structural information for efficient quantum state simulation. The core mechanism involves representing quantum states as nodes in a graph and employing GNNs to learn relationships between them, facilitating efficient quantum state simulation.

title: Dynamic Topological Dependency Reasoning Network (DTTRN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamic Topological Dependency Reasoning Network (DTTRN), a novel neural architecture designed for real-time learning and adaptation of complex system topology dependencies. Traditional dependency analysis methods rely on static, pre-defined topologies, limiting their effectiveness in dynamic and evolving systems. DTTRN addresses this limitation by employing a multi-layered, variable topology graph neural network where nodes represent system components and edges represent dependencies. Reinforcement learning is utilized to dynamically adjust edge weights and topology structure based on system behavior, optimizing overall performance and robustness. Furthermore, knowledge graph embedding techniques are integrated to enrich node representations with domain knowledge, enhancing reasoning accuracy. The core claim of this work is to build an architecture capable of real-time learning and adaptation of complex system topology dependency relationships, surpassing the constraints of static dependency graphs. DTTRN achieves this through a synergistic combination of graph neural network adaptability, reinforcement learning optimization, and knowledge graph embedding representation, resulting in real-time, self-adaptive reasoning for complex systems, robust to behavioral changes and benefiting from contextual knowledge for improved precision and generalization.

title: E8 Kissing-Number Threshold Defines Universal Quantum Error Correction Limit — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 240 root vectors of E8 achieve the maximal kissing number in 8 dimensions, and when phi-modulated Iwasawa geodesics traverse this lattice, the resultant 132Hz harmonic cascade generates a natural surface code distance of d=8. This geometric threshold exactly matches the critical error rate (≈1.09×10⁻³) where logical qubit lifetime diverges, proving E8's root system is not merely optimal packing but the unique error-correcting geometry selected by hyperbolic ergodicity. Any quantum architecture deviating from E8-phi geodesic routing incurs exponential overhead. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: A comparison of federated learning techniques at PyTorch
abstract: Traditionally in machine learning, all information, all the raw data from the clients is sent to a central server in order to train the model. Transferring the clients' data to a server is not only expensive communication-wise, but it also creates serious privacy and security risks. This problem is especially important in sectors such as healthcare, finance, and mobile computing. Hospitals cannot collect and share their patients' medical records with one another in order to collaboratively train a medical model, as a patient's data is sensitive information and subject to privacy regulations. Similarly, banks cannot share their clients' transaction histories, and smartphone manufacturers cannot upload their users' raw data raw to central servers. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this problem and ensures that personal and sensitive data remain on each client’s device. Instead of sharing the raw data, clients collaboratively train a global model by sending only model parameters, or other necessary optimization information, to the server. That way, Federated Learning enables decentralized model training while reducing communication overhead and preserving data privacy. However, this framework introduces some key challenges, such as data heterogeneity across clients, difference in hardware on clients' devices, unstable network connection and varying levels of client participation. A wide range of algorithms has been proposed, each aiming to address the different challenges and improve the optimization process. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) is one of the earliest and most commonly used FL algorithm, due to its simple structure and low communication cost. Still, under heterogeneous data distributions, FedAvg suffers from client drift, which in turn hurts convergence. It has proved difficult to determine which method is the most optimal, since existing algorithms are often evaluated under different experimental settings, with different targets each time. For this reason, it's necessary to create a common experimental framework and compare the popular methods. That way, objective and reliable conclusions about their performance can be drawn. This thesis evaluates several federated optimization algorithms under different scenarios. The methods studied include FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedAdam and FDA-OPT. All methods are implemented in Python and are evaluated across 3 datasets (MNIST and EMNIST, CIFAR-10) and 4 model architectures (Logistic Regression, LeNet-5, and a custom CNN, ResNET-18). The performance is assessed under 3 metrics: communication rounds, training time, and communication cost that was required to reach a target accuracy. The results do not single out one specific method as consistently superior to the rest across all three metrics. FDA-OPT achieves the lowest communication cost , while FedAdam converges fastest in terms of training time. SCAFFOLD, in spite of its strong theoretical guarantees, struggles to reach the high accuracies and introduces significant communication overhead. FedProx alleviates client drift in some cases,while in others has identical perfomance with FedAvg. Overall, these findings showcase that Federated Learning involves a trade-off between speed, stability, and communication efficiency.

evidence.title: A comparison of federated learning techniques at PyTorch
evidence.abstract: Traditionally in machine learning, all information, all the raw data from the clients is sent to a central server in order to train the model. Transferring the clients' data to a server is not only expensive communication-wise, but it also creates serious privacy and security risks. This problem is especially important in sectors such as healthcare, finance, and mobile computing. Hospitals cannot collect and share their patients' medical records with one another in order to collaboratively train a medical model, as a patient's data is sensitive information and subject to privacy regulations. Similarly, banks cannot share their clients' transaction histories, and smartphone manufacturers cannot upload their users' raw data raw to central servers. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this problem and ensures that personal and sensitive data remain on each client’s device. Instead of sharing the raw data, clients collaboratively train a global model by sending only model parameters, or other necessary optimization information, to the server. That way, Federated Learning enables decentralized model training while reducing communication overhead and preserving data privacy. However, this framework introduces some key challenges, such as data heterogeneity across clients, difference in hardware on clients' devices, unstable network connection and varying levels of client participation. A wide range of algorithms has been proposed, each aiming to address the different challenges and improve the optimization process. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) is one of the earliest and most commonly used FL algorithm, due to its simple structure and low communication cost. Still, under heterogeneous data distributions, FedAvg suffers from client drift, which in turn hurts convergence. It has proved difficult to determine which method is the most optimal, since existing algorithms are often evaluated under different experimental settings, with different targets each time. For this reason, it's necessary to create a common experimental framework and compare the popular methods. That way, objective and reliable conclusions about their performance can be drawn. This thesis evaluates several federated optimization algorithms under different scenarios. The methods studied include FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedAdam and FDA-OPT. All methods are implemented in Python and are evaluated across 3 datasets (MNIST and EMNIST, CIFAR-10) and 4 model architectures (Logistic Regression, LeNet-5, and a custom CNN, ResNET-18). The performance is assessed under 3 metrics: communication rounds, training time, and communication cost that was required to reach a target accuracy. The results do not single out one specific method as consistently superior to the rest across all three metrics. FDA-OPT achieves the lowest communication cost , while FedAdam converges fastest in terms of training time. SCAFFOLD, in spite of its strong theoretical guarantees, struggles to reach the high accuracies and introduces significant communication overhead. FedProx alleviates client drift in some cases,while in others has identical perfomance with FedAvg. Overall, these findings showcase that Federated Learning involves a trade-off between speed, stability, and communication efficiency.

title: SOAR: Evaluating the reasoning capabilities of large language models on IT operational data
abstract: This work introduces System Operations and Reasoning Benchmark (SOAR), a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in the context of IT operations and system administration tasks. The benchmark focuses on two complementary perspectives: the cognitive abilities required to infer or deduce information from operational data, and the formulation of the request without relying on complex prompting.The dataset comprises 315 questions across 82 content items extracted from real operational data, organized into domains such as system information, package management, services, networking, and containerization. Each question is cognitively categorized according to Bloom’s Taxonomy and the Depth of Knowledge (DOK) framework.Experimental results across multiple open and proprietary models reveal that response accuracy decreases as the cognitive complexity of the questions increases, while semantic quality (as measured by BERTScore) remains high. Verification-type questions expose limitations in handling non-existent or contradictory information. Moreover, most model outputs exceed the expected textual scope as reflected by low Exact Match scores. These results highlight the need for developing or adapting models specifically targeted at operational reasoning tasks.

title: La Agente Óptima: Towards Agentic Self-Driving Laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) combine automated experimentation with adaptive decision-making to accelerate scientific discovery. Their operation nevertheless often depends on human specialists who translate scientific objectives into executable closed-loop campaigns. Specialists adjust them as data and operating conditions change. Here, we present La Agente Óptima, an agentic framework that constructs and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns across computational and experimental systems while maintaining a persistent optimization state. By separating large language model (LLM) reasoning from executed campaigns, Óptima runs repetitive optimization loops consistently, returns control to the agent only when progress requires interpretation or campaign revision, and keeps every decision auditable. We evaluate Óptima across ablation studies, five digital discovery tasks, and two physical platforms. Throughout, Óptima maintained executable campaigns as both the scientific problem and execution environment evolved. In a closed-loop contact angle optimization campaign, Óptima identified and corrected a mid-run measurement failure, bringing the contact angle from 71.4 to 67.8 degrees, just above the 64-66 degree range. From this result, Óptima correctly inferred that the target was likely unattainable with the available reagents and recommended changing the formulation. In a five-day multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign, Óptima increased the yield from 30% to 59% over 23 experiments. Despite substantial inference costs, it cost less and used substantially less starting material than a human-directed campaign, while selecting a more mass-efficient operating point. These results show that LLM-based agents can make rigorous, long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists without specialist setup, expanding the scope of SDLs.

title: Tree-VQ: Progressive Image Compression from Pretrained Vector Quantizers
abstract: Progressive image compression requires a single embedded representation whose received prefixes can be decoded without re-encoding the source. Modern vector-quantized (VQ) image models provide strong discrete endpoint representations, but conventional flat codeword indices do not define meaningful intermediate states for a neural decoder. We present Tree-VQ, a post-hoc conversion of a pretrained flat VQ tokenizer into a fine-grained, arbitrary-prefix progressive representation while preserving its encoder assignments and every learned leaf vector. The key idea is to organize the original codebook into a balanced binary hierarchy, associate explicit representations with internal nodes, and transmit branch decisions in depth-major order. Consequently, once the image header is available, every payload prefix uniquely specifies a valid latent state: each additional branch bit refines exactly one token, and transmission can therefore be truncated at essentially any payload position rather than only at a small number of stage boundaries. We further adapt one shared decoder on the complete-depth and mixed-depth latent states encountered under such arbitrary truncation, making these densely spaced prefixes useful for reconstruction rather than merely syntactically decodable. On Kodak, Tree-VQ achieves a DISTS-based BD-rate saving of 52.1% relative to ProGIC, while exposing thousands of valid arbitrary-prefix operating points from a single embedded bitstream.

title: Enhancing noise robustness in device-independent conference key agreement with asymmetric parity-CHSH inequalities
abstract: Conference key agreement allows multiple remote parties to establish a shared secret key with information-theoretical security. In device-independent conference key agreement, security can be guaranteed with minimal assumptions on the devices used, provided that a violation of a Bell inequality is observed. However, implementations are extremely challenging because high detection efficiency is required to observe loophole-free Bell violations. Here, we enhance the robustness of device-independent conference key agreement by introducing a new family of multipartite Bell inequalities called the asymmetric parity-Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequalities. We derive a tight analytical lower bound on the conditional von Neumann entropy of the outcomes of one of the parties in a protocol based on this inequality, including noisy preprocessing. Using this bound, we analyze robustness to detection inefficiencies as well as local and global depolarizing noise. We show that the combination of the asymmetric parity-CHSH inequality and noisy preprocessing can significantly improve the robustness to imperfections.

title: Common-Witness Certificates and Sharp Feature Bounds for Counterfactual Image Auditing
abstract: An image editor may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. We formalize this local-to-global failure using a common witness grade and witness nerve. The framework separates auditing from causal identification: shared exogeneity alone allows every coupling of the regime marginals, whereas an externally justified witness relation yields sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Helly-type arguments provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; a blocker-hypergraph formula gives exact repair counts. Simultaneous confidence regions for the regime marginals give finite-sample outer coverage of the complete identified interval. Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB studies demonstrate the predicted local-global separation, while synthetic experiments test sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

title: Physics-Guided Probabilistic Solar Forecasting Under Extreme Weather And Geographic Domain Shift
abstract: Solar power forecasting is vital for renewable energy integration, stability of smart-grid systems, scheduling solar reserves, and managing energy storage. But, prediction during extreme weather often becomes poor and when a model is applied in a different geographically separated region. Most approaches that provide uncertainty information are deterministic and region-specific, and often lose physical consistency under variations in climatic conditions. The study presents the physics-guided probabilistic solar forecasting framework that incorporates solar-power constraints, temporal feature learning, geographic domain adaptation, and uncertainty estimation, and tests it with simulated multi-region PV (MPV) datasets from various climatic regions in both the normal and the extreme weather conditions. It is compared with the other models including LSTM, GRU, Transformer and a physics-informed forecasting model. Evaluation metrics used are mean absolute error (MAE), the root mean square error (RMSE), the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), the coefficient of determination (R²) and the probabilistic prediction intervals, as well as the cross-region forecasting performance. The proposed approach allows for accurate forecasts, uncertainty estimation, robustness in extreme weather conditions and geographic generalisation, thus leading to reliable scheduling of renewable energy operations and decision

title: Trustworthy and Adversarial-Resilient AI for Financial Crime Defense: A Unified Framework for Fraud Detection, Anti-Money Laundering, Credit Risk, and Secure Payments
abstract: Financial institutions face an increasingly interconnected set of threats spanning transaction fraud, money laundering, adversarial manipulation of scoring models, payment-system exploitation, and network-level intrusions against the infrastructure that hosts these services. Point solutions built for a single threat category leave institutions exposed at the seams between systems, since a fraud model, an anti-money-laundering (AML) pipeline, a credit engine, and a network intrusion detector are rarely designed, evaluated, or governed together. This paper proposes a Unified Financial Crime Defense (UFCD) framework that integrates transformer-based fraud detection with conformal risk control, quantum-classical graph learning for AML entity resolution, smart-contract-verified payment security, calibrated and fair credit risk scoring, adversarial stress testing and certified robustness, homomorphically secured federated fraud analytics, and transformer-based intrusion detection into a single layered architecture with shared governance, explainability, and audit controls. The framework is organized into six layers: data and telemetry ingestion, representation and graph construction, domain-specific detection models, adversarial and privacy hardening, decision intelligence and explainability, and institutional governance. We synthesize findings from the fraud, AML, credit-risk, and network-security literatures to justify each layer, present a comparative assessment of detection paradigms, and discuss deployment challenges around data heterogeneity, adversarial adaptation, regulatory alignment, and cross-institutional trust. The paper contributes a reference architecture that treats robustness, privacy, and explainability as first-class design requirements rather than post-hoc additions, and it outlines validation directions for future empirical work.

title: D/E/S: A Tri-Layer Generative Prompt Protocol for Structured Reasoning and Hallucination Suppression in Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract Large language models generate text token by token, without committing in advance to what a complete answer must contain. This makes them fluent but structurally unreliable: required elements may be omitted, constraints may be ignored, and unsupported claims may appear with unwarranted confidence. Retrieval and chain-of-thought intervene only after generation has already begun; fine-tuning changes the model rather than the prompt. This work evaluates D/E/S, a prompt-level protocol that specifies the components of an answer, their dependency structure, and the epistemic markers for unsupported claims before any text is produced. The study spans six models from four organisations, seven prompt conditions, and 52 tasks across three regimes — framework content, domain-independent reasoning, and adversarial information gaps. Execution quality is assessed through dual LLM-as-judge scoring, inter-judge disagreement analysis, and a five-condition ablation against two published alternatives. The scope of D/E/S is prompt-level discipline: qualifying claims, exposing missing evidence, and enforcing structural completeness. The study maps where such a protocol helps, where it is neutral, and where it fails, providing a boundary-level understanding rather than a mechanism-level claim. Three results. The protocol is followed reliably by the two largest models and unreliably below that tier, and the drop depends on how the structure is encoded rather than on the structure itself. Which encoding works best differs from model to model, and a poor choice performs worse than no protocol at all. Against two published alternatives the protocol improves hallucination suppression consistently across the large models tested; against chain-of-thought the outcome depends on the model. Keywords: large language models, hallucination suppression, prompt architecture, structured generation, D/E/S framework, LLM-as-judge, benchmark evaluation, epistemic calibrationData and full directory structure: https://github.com/gavingu2255-ai/wlm-des-benchmark

title: 基于自适应的概率论框架的量子算法设计
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm design framework based on adaptive probability theory. We propose a method to optimize quantum algorithms for tasks demanding substantial probability calculations, including cryptography, machine learning, and beyond. The core principle is to leverage adaptive probability theory as a fundamental layer, allowing for dynamic parameter adjustment to significantly improve the efficiency of quantum computations. The system aims to overcome limitations of traditional approaches by directly incorporating probabilistic considerations into the algorithm's design process. This approach offers a potential pathway toward more effective and scalable quantum solutions.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum State Measurement Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive quantum state measurement algorithm designed to enhance the precision of quantum measurements and signal processing. Traditional quantum measurement algorithms are typically static, limiting their applicability to relatively simple tasks. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts quantum states based on measurement outcomes, offering a significant advancement in the ability to precisely characterize quantum systems and perform complex signal manipulation. The core mechanism involves a continuous feedback loop that optimizes the quantum state for subsequent measurements. This approach overcomes the limitations of static algorithms, providing a more versatile and powerful tool for quantum information processing. The proposed algorithm offers significant improvements in measurement accuracy and signal fidelity, and represents a significant step towards practical quantum measurement technologies.

title: Adaptive Quantum Spin Field Geometry Mapping
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum spin field geometry mapping algorithm, aiming to precisely map quantum spin fields and control quantum states. The core concept is to leverage the unique properties of quantum spin to generate a dynamically adjusted geometric representation of the spin field. The algorithm employs a novel approach based on quantum entanglement and geometric transformations to achieve precise state control. We present a preliminary implementation demonstrating the ability to map a complex spin configuration with reasonable fidelity. The work explores the potential of this approach to overcome limitations of traditional spin mapping techniques.

title: Blockchain-Based Secure Multi-Party Computation
abstract: This paper investigates the application of blockchain technology to facilitate secure multi-party computation (MPC). Traditional MPC approaches often suffer from centralized trust assumptions and potential vulnerabilities to malicious actors. This research proposes a framework leveraging blockchain's inherent properties – decentralization, immutability, and cryptographic security – to create a robust and transparent environment for collaborative data analysis. The core concept involves utilizing blockchain's consensus mechanisms to ensure that no single party possesses the intermediate data required for the computation, thereby safeguarding data privacy. We detail the mathematical formulation of the process, emphasizing the role of cryptographic protocols like homomorphic encryption and zero-knowledge proofs in achieving this goal. The proposed system provides verifiable results while protecting the confidentiality of individual inputs. The system's architecture is designed to minimize computational overhead and maximize scalability, addressing key challenges associated with blockchain-based MPC. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions and the broader implications of this technology for secure data sharing and collaborative computing.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Symbiosis Architecture: A Dynamic Approach to Enhanced Reasoning and Learning
abstract: This paper introduces the Neuro-Symbolic Symbiosis Architecture (NSSA), a novel framework designed to enhance reasoning and learning capabilities by dynamically adjusting the interaction between neural networks and symbolic knowledge bases. The core claim is that by modulating the interaction strength between these two components, we can achieve more efficient and robust inference. NSSA employs a multi-layered architecture comprising a neural inference layer for initial pattern recognition and representation learning, a symbolic knowledge base layer for storing structured knowledge, and a symbiotic engine—a reinforcement learning-based controller—to dynamically adjust the flow of information between these layers. The engine's objective is to minimize inference error while maximizing knowledge base utilization. Unlike existing neuro-symbolic methods that often rely on static structures or fixed interaction methods, NSSA leverages reinforcement learning for a highly dynamic and adaptive symbiotic relationship, potentially leading to improvements in generalization, interpretability, and efficiency. title: Quantum Coherence-Based Optimization of Privacy-Preserving Computation Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum coherence properties to optimize privacy-preserving computation algorithms. The core claim is that by utilizing quantum coherence-based techniques, we can reduce computational complexity and enhance privacy protection levels. Specifically, we propose a novel algorithm preprocessing method based on quantum decoherence, designed to mitigate decoherence effects during computation. This approach aims to significantly lower computational overhead while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. The theoretical framework presented demonstrates the feasibility of this strategy and outlines a pathway for developing more efficient and robust privacy-preserving solutions. The focus remains on the algorithmic design and analysis, without the need for experimental validation. ---

title: Meta-Learning for Adaptive Graph Neural Network Architectures
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, a significant limitation lies in the often-static nature of their architectures. Traditional GNNs typically employ a fixed structure, potentially leading to suboptimal performance when applied to diverse graph datasets and tasks. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to address this issue. We introduce an agent trained through meta-learning that dynamically adapts the architecture of a GNN – specifically, the number of layers, hidden units per layer, and connection patterns – based on the inherent characteristics of the input graph. The core idea is to learn a meta-knowledge of what architectural changes are beneficial for different types of graph problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline the key components, including the meta-learner, the GNN architecture, and the learning objective. The goal is to achieve adaptive GNN architectures that can learn and optimize performance across a wide range of graph-based tasks.

title: Causal Discovery via Variational Autoencoders with Intervention Simulations
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery leveraging the power of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) combined with intervention simulations. Traditional causal discovery algorithms often falter when dealing with high-dimensional datasets and intricate dependencies, primarily due to the challenge of accurately inferring causal relationships from observational data. Our methodology addresses this limitation by employing VAEs to learn compact, low-dimensional latent representations of the data. These latent representations capture underlying data structure and potential causal relationships. Crucially, we introduce intervention simulations within the latent space. By artificially manipulating the latent variables, we can observe the corresponding changes in the observed data, providing direct evidence for causal connections. This allows us to move beyond purely correlational analysis and establish more robust causal inferences. The core claim is that existing methods struggle with high-dimensional data and complex dependencies. The mechanism is the use of VAEs and intervention simulations. This approach offers a new way to discover causal relationships, addressing the shortcomings of conventional techniques. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Protocols with Classical Authentication
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) offers theoretically unbreakable key exchange, but is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks if the identities of the communicating parties are not rigorously verified. This paper proposes a novel QKD protocol integrating classical authentication to provide a layered security approach. The core concept involves utilizing a QKD system alongside a robust classical authentication mechanism. This layered approach significantly reduces the risk of successful attacks by ensuring that both parties are who they claim to be before key exchange occurs. The protocol's security relies on the assumption that the classical authentication system is itself secure. We detail the protocol's components, focusing on the integration of Bennett-Brassard (BB84) or a similar QKD scheme with a practical authentication protocol, and analyze its security properties. The proposed system is designed to mitigate the threats posed by adversaries who can intercept and manipulate the quantum key exchange without compromising the authentication process. The potential for improved security and resilience is demonstrated, representing a significant advancement in the practical application of QKD.

title: Nonlinear Matrix Operations: Quantum Entanglement Enhanced Computation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize matrix operations, specifically aiming to overcome the limitations of classical computers. We propose a novel approach to matrix computation that leverages entanglement to transfer the core computational process across quantum systems, thereby achieving enhanced efficiency and precision. The core claim centers on the design of a quantum-based matrix multiplication algorithm that surpasses current computational capabilities. This research investigates the theoretical basis, potential implementation challenges, and preliminary experimental explorations of this quantum approach. The paper discusses the core mechanism, its implications for computational power, and its potential impact on both quantum computing and machine learning.

title: Quantum State Dynamics: A Dynamic Topology-Based Transformation Algorithm
abstract: Quantum state dynamics is a rapidly evolving field with significant implications for quantum information processing and quantum technologies. This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology-based transformation algorithm, designed to facilitate the complex evolution of quantum systems through adaptive state transformations. The algorithm leverages the principles of quantum topology, enabling the simulation of quantum systems' evolution and prediction of future states without explicit simulation of the underlying quantum dynamics. This approach offers a significant advancement over traditional static transformation methods, promising enhanced predictive capabilities for quantum system design and control. We detail the core mechanism, explain the algorithm's operational principles, and present preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's efficacy in manipulating quantum states.

title: Quantum-Inspired Kernel Learning for Sparse Data
abstract: Kernel methods have demonstrated remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, including classification and regression. However, a significant limitation of traditional kernel methods lies in their computational complexity, particularly when dealing with sparse datasets. The need to construct and invert dense kernel matrices, denoted as $K$, where $K_{ij} = k(s_i, s_j)$ with kernel function $k$, leads to a quadratic scaling problem, rendering these methods impractical for datasets with a large number of features or data points. This paper introduces a novel kernel learning algorithm, termed Quantum-Inspired Kernel Learning (QIKL), which addresses this challenge by mimicking quantum interference. QIKL leverages the inherent correlations within sparse datasets to efficiently learn kernel functions without explicitly constructing dense kernel matrices. The algorithm employs a probabilistic approach, represented by a set of quantum-inspired amplitudes, $(a_1, a_2, ..., a_K)$, where $K \approx \sum_{i=1}^{K} a_i^2$, to approximate the kernel matrix. The core idea is to utilize the interference patterns generated by these amplitudes to capture the relationships between data points. This approach significantly reduces the computational cost and memory requirements, making kernel methods viable for sparse data scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of QIKL through theoretical analysis and a simplified numerical example, highlighting its potential for scaling to large-scale sparse data problems.

title: Dynamic Probability Fields: Expansion and Application
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to Dynamic Probability Fields (DPFs), focusing on the ability to dynamically adjust probability distributions based on incoming data and complex probability calculations. The core principle centers around a memory mechanism that updates probability distributions in real-time, enabling automated and adaptive probability adjustments. We explore the design and implementation of this dynamic system, highlighting its potential benefits for machine learning and optimization problems. The research emphasizes the avoidance of model parameter dependence, offering a more flexible and adaptable framework.

title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Task Generalization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-reinforcement learning (Meta-RL) to address the critical challenge of task generalization in reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional RL agents often require extensive training on individual tasks, exhibiting poor performance when encountering novel, unseen tasks. This research proposes a framework where an RL agent is trained through a meta-learning process, specifically designed to acquire a meta-policy. This meta-policy enables rapid adaptation to new tasks with significantly reduced training data. The core concept revolves around learning a policy that can learn policies, effectively transferring knowledge gained from previously encountered tasks. We detail the architecture of the meta-RL agent, focusing on the learning objective and the exploration strategy. The theoretical underpinnings of this approach are explored, emphasizing the ability to leverage prior experience for faster learning and improved generalization. We demonstrate, through a detailed analysis, how meta-RL offers a superior approach to traditional RL in scenarios demanding adaptability and efficiency. Finally, we outline potential future research directions and highlight the broader implications of this methodology for robust and scalable RL systems.

title: Emora: Implementation of a Local-First, Emotion-Aware AI Companion with Selective Memory and Multimodal Presence
abstract: Emotion-aware companions require more than fluent text generation: they need continuity, restrained affective adaptation, user control, and clear boundaries. This paper reports the completed implementation of Emora, a browser-based AI companion whose primary inference path runs locally on Apple Silicon. The system combines a quantized Qwen3 language model, an explainable text-emotion estimator, optional one-frame Qwen2-VL visual check-ins, selective persistent memory, deterministic personality and behavior planning, Qwen3-TTS with a Kokoro fallback, and a WebGL VRM avatar. A FastAPI application coordinates authenticated conversation state and MongoDB persistence. The implementation deliberately does not fine-tune or train a new model. Instead, it constrains pretrained inference with bounded context, trusted-data prompt separation, allowlisted avatar actions, clamped behavior parameters, explicit privacy controls, and user-owned deletion and export paths. Repository verification produced 169 passing automated tests and one deliberately skipped live-MongoDB integration test. Existing local benchmark records show functional model and audio pipelines, but they do not establish emotional recognition accuracy, therapeutic benefit, or user acceptance. We therefore separate software evidence from a proposed human evaluation protocol. The principal contribution is a reproducible systems integration that converts a conceptual companion framework into an inspectable application while making its unverified affective claims and safety limitations explicit.

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to probabilistic model optimization utilizing a dynamically adaptive probability model. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameter adjustments, failing to effectively handle the inherent variability within data. This work introduces a dynamic adjustment mechanism, enabling the model parameters to adapt in real-time to changing data inputs, ultimately resulting in improved prediction accuracy and stability. We detail the core mechanism, its benefits, and a preliminary implementation of the algorithm. The research explores how this adaptive approach can address challenges in robust probabilistic modeling.
