title: Symbolic Logic and Reinforcement Learning Hybrid Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper introduces a novel hybrid reasoning engine that integrates symbolic logic and reinforcement learning (RL). The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both paradigms: symbolic logic for precise knowledge representation and deductive reasoning, and reinforcement learning for adaptive exploration and reward-based learning. We propose a mechanism where an RL agent learns to infer rules from a symbolic knowledge base, and subsequently utilizes these rules to guide its exploration within an environment. This synergistic approach aims to overcome limitations of purely symbolic or purely reinforcement learning systems, resulting in a more robust and flexible reasoning capability. The engine is designed to handle complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments where traditional approaches may struggle. We present a framework for this hybrid engine and discuss its potential applications.

We present a framework that incorporates a dynamic mapping strategy, incorporating a feedback loop to improve performance across challenging regions. The core mechanism centers around a layered approach: initial parameter setting, gradient-based adjustment, noise-aware refinement, and a final evaluation step. The proposed algorithm demonstrates significant improvements in optimization performance compared to established techniques, particularly in scenarios involving complex landscapes and noisy objective functions. The paper concludes with a detailed discussion of the algorithm's design and results, highlighting its potential for broader applicability across diverse optimization challenges.

title: Unsupervised NLP for quantifying sentiment deviation and framing in global climate discourse
abstract: Climate change news coverage varies by region and media organization. These differences show in the way news is framed, the themes chosen, and communication priorities. This study suggests a scalable and unsupervised natural language processing (NLP) framework to measure sentiment changes and framing patterns in global climate discussions across major news outlets. The proposed system uses Zero-Shot BART-large-MNLI as the main sentiment classification model, while VADER serves as a comparative baseline during model validation. Key themes are identified using BERTopic. We detect changes in climate narratives over time with the Pruned Exact Linear Time (PELT) changepoint detection algorithm. We introduce a dual-baseline framework to calculate relative sentiment changes. This combines regional consensus with a scientific baseline. It allows comparison of framing patterns without hiding systematic regional differences. The BART-MNLI model was tested against a manually annotated sample of articles. It achieved an accuracy of 98.0%, an F1-score of 0.98, and Cohen’s κ of 0.96, showing strong agreement with human annotations. It significantly outperformed lexicon-based sentiment analysis for professional news text. We also assessed statistical robustness with the Kruskal-Wallis H-test, bootstrap confidence intervals, and PELT sensitivity analysis. The framework reveals regional sentiment differences, outlet-level framing patterns, thematic trends, and notable shifts in response to major climate events. It offers a clear, reproducible, and flexible method for analyzing global climate communication.

title: Effect of monitoring prompts on help-seeking with an AI-based learning assistant
abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of metacognitive monitoring prompts in promoting instrumental help-seeking behaviors (Nelson-Le Gall, 1981, 1985; Newman, 1994) when interacting with a generative artificial intelligence-based learning assistant. It also investigates their effects on learner performance in the context of an online training course on cognitive biases and misinformation. Help-seeking, recognized as a key self-regulated learning strategy (Karabenick & Berger, 2013; Zimmerman, 2000), can be distinguished into instrumental help-seeking (seeking clarification, associated with better performance) and executive help-seeking (directly obtaining an answer, negatively associated with performance; Aleven et al., 2016). Detecting the need for help relies in part on the accuracy of metacognitive monitoring, which varies substantially across individuals (Chu et al., 2018). Several meta-analyses support the effectiveness of metacognitive prompts (external cues or triggers designed to guide learners through their self-regulatory processes by directing their attention, reflections, strategies, or actions during learning (Bannert et al., 2009)) in improving learners' self-regulated learning behaviors and performance in online learning environments (Guo, 2022; Guan et al., 2025). Here, we test their effectiveness in specifically supporting instrumental help-seeking when interacting with an AI-based learning assistant. We will also examine whether these effects are moderated by learners' socioeconomic status (SES), based on two competing hypotheses, with no a priori predicted direction. On the one hand, a compensatory effect may emerge, whereby prompts compensate for the lower levels of self-regulation generally associated with lower SES (Storksen et al., 2014). On the other hand, a second-order digital divide effect may occur, whereby higher-SES learners are better equipped to take advantage of digital help resources (Fan, 2025; Van Dijk, 2005). Participants (N = 600), recruited through Prolific and randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions (between-subjects design), will complete a short online training course (15–20 minutes) on the Didask learning platform. The platform integrates an AI-based learning assistant that learners can use to better understand a concept, obtain a reformulation, or request an example when needed. In the experimental condition, metacognitive monitoring prompts will invite learners to assess the extent to which they feel capable of explaining various key points from the content they have just encountered to someone else. If they identify a need for clarification, reformulation, or an example, they will then be encouraged to seek assistance from the learning assistant. In the control condition, learners will not receive any monitoring prompts. Instead, they will be reminded of the possibility of using the assistant and informed about its functionalities. We will therefore test whether these prompts increase the use of the assistant for instrumental help-seeking purposes and whether such use constitutes a mechanism through which the prompts improve learner performance. Finally, we will examine whether these effects vary as a function of learners' socioeconomic status (SES).

title: Path analysis of students’ aesthetic education and individualized construction of career guidance based on fuzzy logic
abstract: This research focuses on path analysis of students’ aesthetic education and individualized construction of career guidance based on fuzzy logic. Unlike conventional fuzzy recommendation systems that merely apply fixed rule bases, this study explicitly addresses three limitations of existing approaches: (a) static rule bases that do not incorporate periodic feedback from student outcomes; (b) absence of domain-specific rule design grounded in aesthetic education theory; and (c) lack of interpretable linkage between aesthetic education inputs and career guidance outputs. The proposed system integrates a fuzzy inference engine with a dynamic feedback loop that adjusts membership function parameters based on periodic student re-evaluations. Experimental results show that the model achieves 83.2% top-1 accuracy, which is comparable to existing fuzzy recommenders, but with the added advantage of providing rule-level explanations for each recommendation. The contribution lies not in claiming novelty of fuzzy logic itself, but in tailoring the rule structure and feedback mechanism specifically to the aesthetic education domain, which has been underexplored in prior fuzzy recommendation literature.

title: Structural Frontiers in Constructed Systems: Domains of Validity and Emergent Structural Effects
abstract: ABSTRACT Persistent patterns of confinement, sensitivity to initialization and diminishing qualitative returns from increasingly sophisticated tuning strategies are widely reported across heuristic search and optimization contexts. These phenomena are commonly interpreted as algorithmic shortcomings, motivating successive layers of stochasticity, parameter refinement or hybridization. This paper frames persistent heuristic behaviour as an emergent property of admissibility structures and boundary judgements defined ex ante in constructed systems, rather than as a failure of local search dynamics. Instead of treating heuristics as the primary object of analysis, the paper places the structure of constructed search spaces defined ex ante at the centre of inquiry. We introduce a minimal, deliberately simple search space in which a boundary separating locally accessible regions is identifiable prior to any algorithmic intervention. This boundary (termed an energetic barrier) arises from the joint specification of the state space, locality assumptions and admissible transitions, and is independent of operator design choices. The paper further formalizes the distinct, stronger notion of a structural frontier, arising directly from the admissibility mapping rather than from the cost structure, and clarifies the conditions under which each applies. Using this construction, we analyse three classes of responses commonly observed in practice: baseline local exploration, epistemological refinement through parameterized stochastic search and landscape transformation via objective deformation. The analysis shows that refinement‐based responses systematically preserve the set of admissible transitions, improving exploration only within regions already accessible under the assumed structure. Apparent resolution of confinement emerges only when the admissibility structure or effective representation of the space is altered, thereby redefining the problem rather than traversing the original barrier. Persistence under refinement and apparent success under transformation constitute complementary diagnostic signals of underlying structural constraints. The contribution of this work is not a new optimization method, but a diagnostic framework for distinguishing algorithmic difficulty from structural inadmissibility in constructed systems. By shifting attention from operators to admissibility boundaries, the paper offers implications for the design, interpretation and governance of optimization systems, and contributes to broader discussions in systems thinking concerning boundary setting, problem representation and the limits of intervention.

title: Seeing Before Synthesizing: VLM-Guided Transition Event Discovery for Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning
abstract: Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning aims to localize and describe multiple events in untrimmed videos given only an ordered set of event-level captions per video. Recent work synthesizes auxiliary transition captions via LLM to provide additional vision-language alignment, but these captions lack visual grounding and are rigidly assigned to every inter-event gap at a fixed location and duration. To address these, we propose Seeing Before Synthesizing (SBS), a framework that adaptively provides visually grounded linguistic guidance only where warranted. Leveraging a VLM, we generate frame-level narratives for the inter-event gaps and detect transitions from the semantic variation across them. For identified transitions, we then refine inter-event temporal masks by blending the temporal midpoint with the semantic change point and selecting the width that maximizes vision-language alignment. Experiments on ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both captioning and localization.

title: Bernstein--von Mises theorems for Bayesian probabilistic numerics
abstract: We study probabilistic numerical methods for solving nonlinear PDEs from a Bayesian nonparametric perspective. Given noisy evaluations at random collocation points, we place a truncated Gaussian series prior on the unknown solution and establish contraction at the minimax nonparametric rate, up to a logarithmic factor. Our main results give Gaussian approximations of the posterior in positive-order Sobolev spaces and, under suitable conditions, in the uniform topology. This contrasts with classical ill-posed inverse problems, where Bernstein--von Mises theorems typically require substantially weaker topologies. Here, the observation operator is differential rather than smoothing, and inversion of its linearisation gains regularity, making these strong-topology results possible. The posterior may be centred at either the posterior mean or the posterior mode. We further prove that the Gaussian Laplace approximation is asymptotically equivalent to the true posterior at a $\sqrt{N}$-scale.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
abstract: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

title: On Global Regulatability of Robot Manipulators by Classical PID
abstract: A long-standing open problem in robot manipulator control is whether global regulation can be achieved by classical PID control. This paper provides an answer to this question for classical PID controllers with triple parameters (k_p,k_i,k_d) in R^3. We find and prove that for one-degree-of-freedom manipulators, the classical PID control guarantees global stability and asymptotic regulation under standard structural assumptions, and further derive explicit quantitative design conditions for the PID gains. However, for multi-degree-of-freedom cases, we can construct a robot manipulator satisfying the same structural assumptions for which no choice of PID gains (k_p,k_i,k_d) can achieve global asymptotic regulation. These results provide a fundamental understanding of the abovementioned open problem, revealing both the fundamental capability and intrinsic limitation of the classical PID control for robot manipulator dynamics.

title: Quantum Simulation Adaptive Geometry Transformation
abstract: This paper explores the development of a novel quantum simulation framework centered around dynamic geometric transformation adjustment. Traditional quantum simulation often necessitates manual parameter tuning, limiting flexibility and potentially impacting accuracy. We propose a quantum geometric technique, leveraging quantum states to iteratively refine geometric transformations during the simulation process, resulting in improved accuracy and reduced computational burden. The core mechanism focuses on employing quantum states to represent and manipulate geometric primitives, allowing for adaptive and optimized transformations. This framework addresses the limitations of conventional methods, offering a promising pathway towards more efficient and accurate quantum simulations.

title: Adaptive Topological Genetic Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive topological genetic algorithm (ATGA) designed to efficiently find optimal solutions and maintain stability and reliability. Traditional genetic algorithms often suffer from the tendency to get trapped in local optima, while the ATGA leverages topological structure to promote global optimality. The algorithm employs a novel approach that constructs and maintains a topological representation of the search space, dynamically adjusting the search space to avoid these local optima. This paper details the algorithm's structure, proposes a mechanism for ensuring stability and reliability, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its performance.

title: Title: Adaptive Geometric Transformations for Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for revolutionizing various fields, from drug discovery to materials science. However, realizing this potential requires efficient and scalable quantum algorithms. This paper explores the application of adaptive geometric transformations as a core mechanism for enhancing the performance of quantum computations. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts geometric parameters during the computation process, aiming to achieve higher fidelity and reduced computational complexity. The core claim is that this approach significantly improves the efficiency of quantum algorithms, particularly in scenarios involving complex quantum circuits. The paper details the design of the adaptive transformation function, its implementation within a quantum computing framework, and a preliminary analysis of its impact on key quantum algorithms. The study demonstrates the efficacy of this approach through simulations and a simplified demonstration of a specific quantum circuit. The research contributes to the ongoing development of robust and adaptable quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum Topological Networks
abstract: Quantum Topological Networks (QTNs) represent a revolutionary paradigm shift in quantum information processing, offering potential for unparalleled computational speeds and secure communication. This paper explores the fundamental principles of QTNs, focusing on the utilization of quantum entanglement to construct a robust and efficient network for complex calculations and data transmission. The core claim of this work is that a meticulously engineered QTN architecture, leveraging the unique properties of entangled qubits, will dramatically enhance the performance of quantum computations compared to existing approaches. We detail the proposed mechanism, emphasizing the critical role of quantum entanglement in facilitating information transfer and computation. The significance of this research lies in its potential to unlock transformative capabilities across diverse quantum applications.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Nonlinear System Simulation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a unique approach to simulating complex nonlinear systems. This research explores the design of a novel simulation framework leveraging quantum entanglement to achieve enhanced accuracy and efficiency in modeling these systems. We propose a system that utilizes quantum algorithms to meticulously capture the dynamics of the system, providing precise simulation and predictive capabilities. This work addresses the limitations of traditional simulation methods, particularly in handling intricate non-linear systems, and presents a fundamentally new approach to this challenging problem. The core mechanism centers on exploiting entanglement to create a more stable and accurate representation of the system's behavior. This paper outlines the design of the framework, its potential applications, and preliminary results demonstrating its efficacy in simulating specific nonlinear systems.

title: The Adaptive Quantum Computation Algorithm via Dynamic Topology Adjustment
abstract: Quantum computation, a fundamentally different approach to computation, offers the potential for unparalleled speed and complexity. Traditional algorithms often rely on fixed, static parameters, limiting their adaptability to diverse inputs. This paper introduces a novel adaptive quantum computation algorithm based on dynamic topology adjustment, designed to overcome these limitations. We propose a framework that dynamically modifies the quantum system's topology during computation, allowing it to adapt to varying input conditions and enhance its robustness. The core mechanism involves employing a sophisticated mapping function to translate the input state into a specific topology, effectively tailoring the quantum system's response. This adaptive approach significantly improves the algorithm's ability to handle complex problems and maintain consistent performance across a range of inputs. The proposed algorithm demonstrates improved results through rigorous analysis and simulations, showcasing its potential for advancing the field of quantum computation.

The core mechanism involves simulating intricate geometric structures, generating candidate solutions, and employing geometric optimization techniques to refine the search process. We present a framework demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in optimizing a specific geometric function, showcasing its potential for broader applicability across diverse problems.

title: Quantum Hiding Matrix Adaptive Optimization
abstract: Quantum Hiding Matrix Adaptive Optimization is a novel optimization framework designed to enhance the robustness and adaptability of machine learning models through the utilization of quantum mechanics. title: Context-Aware Graph Neural Networks for Social Network Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Context-Aware Graph Neural Networks (CAGNNs) for enhancing social network analysis. Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) primarily focus on the structural relationships within a network, often overlooking crucial contextual information that significantly influences social dynamics. This research argues that incorporating user demographics, location data, and social group affiliations as contextual features dramatically improves the accuracy and interpretability of GNN models. We propose a framework where the standard graph structure is augmented with these contextual attributes, and GNNs are trained to learn representations sensitive to both the network's topology and the associated contextual nuances. Through this approach, we aim to move beyond purely structural analysis, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of social networks and their complexities. We present a detailed formulation of the CAGNN model and discuss key considerations for its implementation and evaluation. The results presented demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual information into GNNs, showcasing its ability to capture richer social relationships and improve predictive performance.

title: 基于自适应的动态扰动算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic perturbation algorithm designed to enhance model training and prediction efficiency. Traditional perturbation methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their adaptability to evolving data. Our algorithm leverages a self-adaptive approach, meticulously learning the inherent characteristics of input data perturbations. This learning process dynamically adjusts model parameters, resulting in improved performance across a wider range of scenarios. The core mechanism centers around a continuous feedback loop, optimizing parameter adjustments based on observed data fluctuations. This adaptation allows the algorithm to effectively handle data variability and improve the model's robustness. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experimental results on a diverse dataset of image processing and regression tasks. The key contribution is the incorporation of a robust learning mechanism that ensures the algorithm's adaptability and performance remain consistent even with significant data shifts.

title: Quantum Tunneling-Based Algorithm Acceleration
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to algorithm acceleration by leveraging the principles of quantum tunneling. The core idea is to map specific computational steps within classical algorithms onto simulated quantum tunneling processes. By employing probability calculations and sampling techniques, we aim to achieve significant speedups for certain algorithms. This work presents a theoretical framework and outlines a methodology for implementing this approach, focusing on the potential advantages offered by quantum mechanics in overcoming limitations inherent in classical computation. The exploration includes detailed mathematical formulations and conceptual descriptions, offering a foundation for future research and development in this area. We demonstrate the feasibility of this method through illustrative examples, highlighting the potential for transformative gains in computational efficiency. The focus remains on the theoretical aspects and algorithmic design, without requiring experimental validation. ---

title: Responsibility-Space Contracts for Assuring Adaptive AI: Design-Derived Responsibility Boundaries and Selective Formal Assurance — Research Artifact
abstract: Research artifact accompanying the manuscript “Responsibility-Space Contracts for Assuring Adaptive AI: Design-Derived Responsibility Boundaries and Selective Formal Assurance.” The artifact contains the implementation and frozen evaluation evidence supporting RQ2–RQ5, including responsibility-level contract evaluation, bounded neural-network verification, modified-model evaluation, and edge-platform evaluation on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 5. The artifact is distributed as a frozen package with a SHA-256 integrity manifest and claim-to-evidence mapping. Selected DTLD-derived inputs, including redistributed tensor caches and detailed sanitized holdout data, are excluded because redistribution permission has not been established. The included evidence supports the claims and experimental scope reported in the accompanying manuscript. In particular, bounded neural-network verification results are case-local and should not be interpreted as a universal robustness guarantee, and the edge-platform measurements should not be interpreted as a general hardware-ranking claim.

title: Quantum Entanglement Field Topology
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing communication and computation. However, the inherent fragility of entangled states presents significant challenges for reliable data transmission. This paper investigates the use of topological quantum field theory to enhance quantum entanglement, proposing a novel framework centered around dynamically constructed topological structures. We explore how these structures can bolster the stability and transfer capability of entangled states, offering a potential pathway to more robust and efficient quantum communication and computation. The core claim is that the integration of dynamic topology into quantum entanglement will yield a significant improvement in these areas. This work presents a theoretical framework based on the principles of self-similarity and the manipulation of topological properties. The investigation will focus on creating a quantum field topology that facilitates stable entanglement, leading to enhanced data security and computational speed.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Parallel Transport for Quantum State Preservation
abstract: Quantum state preservation is a fundamental challenge in quantum information theory, particularly when dealing with complex systems and measurement. Traditional methods often rely on approximations that can introduce errors. This paper proposes a novel method for preserving quantum states through non-Euclidean parallel transport, offering a potential breakthrough in maintaining the integrity of quantum states. We introduce a 'Quantum State Morphing Algorithm' designed to minimize geometric distortions during transport, leading to enhanced state preservation. We detail the algorithm's principles, explore its theoretical implications, and present preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness in preserving quantum states. This work addresses a critical need in quantum information theory, offering a viable path toward more robust and reliable quantum computations.

title: Title: Dynamic Topology-Based Machine Learning Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel machine learning optimization algorithm based on dynamic topology. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter adjustments, which can limit the algorithm's ability to adapt to complex data distributions. This work proposes a dynamic topology-based approach that iteratively optimizes model parameters by simulating data distribution, resulting in enhanced model performance. The core mechanism involves utilizing a dynamic topology structure to guide parameter adjustments, enabling the algorithm to effectively explore the data space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and generalization ability.
